hypothesis: Higher mitotic count per mm² correlates with upregulation of cell cycle–related genes and poorer survival in SKCM patients.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Assess association between mitotic rate, expression of cell cycle genes, and survival outcomes.

Steps: 1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv.
2. Identify cell cycle gene set (e.g., CCNA2, CCNB1, CDK1, MKI67) and extract their expression values.
3. Compute cell cycle score per patient as mean expression of selected genes.
4. Merge with mitotic_count_per_mm2 and survival data.
5. Compute Pearson correlation between mitotic_count_per_mm2 and cell cycle score; report r and p-value.
6. Fit Cox model: time/event ~ mitotic_count_per_mm2 + cell_cycle_score + age_at_diagnosis.
7. Report HRs for mitotic count and cell cycle score, with 95% CIs and p-values.
8. Plot scatter of mitotic count vs cell cycle score with regression line, and Kaplan–Meier curves stratified by high/low cell cycle score.

Deliverables: • Correlation coefficient and p-value
• Cox model summary with HRs and p-values
• Scatter plot of mitotic count vs cell cycle score
• Kaplan–Meier plots for high vs low cell cycle score
analysis:
The code executed all planned steps without errors, and the key findings are:

1. Pearson correlation: r=0.076 (p=0.330), indicating a very weak, non‐significant positive correlation between mitotic count per mm² and cell cycle score.

2. Cox proportional hazards model (N≈316 patients):
   • Mitotic count per mm²: HR=1.03 (95% CI 1.00–1.06), p=0.025 — higher mitotic count is significantly associated with worse survival.
   • Cell cycle score: HR=0.87 (95% CI 0.65–1.20), p=0.404 — no significant effect on survival after adjusting for age.

3. Scatter plot confirms a weak positive trend between mitotic count and cell cycle score.

4. Kaplan–Meier curves stratified by median cell cycle score show the “High” group with lower survival probability over time, though formal log‐rank p‐value was not reported.

Overall, mitotic count per mm² correlates poorly with the mean expression of selected cell cycle genes but independently predicts worse survival. Cell cycle score alone did not reach significance in the multivariable survival model.

hypothesis: Melanoma patients harboring BRAF mutations undergo fewer treatment courses (as approximated by available treatment‐indicator variables) and exhibit altered expression of key immune checkpoint genes (PDCD1, CD274, CTLA4) compared to BRAF wild‐type patients.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Quantify and compare treatment burden—derived from existing clinical treatment indicators—and checkpoint gene expression between BRAF‐mutant and wild‐type melanoma patients.

Steps: 1. Load the three datasets: cleaned_clinical_data.csv, cleaned_mutations.csv, cleaned_gene_expression.csv.
2. In the mutation data, mark any patient with at least one Hugo_Symbol=='BRAF' mutation as “Mutant”; label all others “Wild‐type”. Match patient IDs by taking the first 12 characters of the Tumor_Sample_Barcode or patient_id.
3. Merge this BRAF status into the clinical table via submitter_id→patient_id.
4. From clinical data, build a treatment burden score per patient by summing six binary fields: prior_systemic_therapy, prior_radiation_therapy, radiation_therapy, radiation_to_primary, history_neoadjuvant, and interferon_90d_prior_excision. Code “YES”=1, “NO” or missing=0.  
5. For the two groups, compute descriptive statistics (mean, median, IQR) of the treatment burden score. Test for differences using a two‐sided Mann–Whitney U test.  
6. Create a bar chart of mean burden score (with standard‐error or standard‐deviation bars) and a boxplot of its full distribution across BRAF groups.
7. In the gene expression matrix, isolate rows for PDCD1, CD274, CTLA4 (map Ensembl|symbol index to the symbol). Collapse sample‐level expression to patient‐level by averaging all samples (first 12 characters of column name).
8. Merge resulting patient‐level checkpoint expression with BRAF status.
9. For each gene, perform a two‐sample Welch’s t‐test comparing Mutant vs. Wild‐type. Collect raw p‐values and adjust via Benjamini–Hochberg FDR.
10. Visualize expression differences: a separate boxplot for each checkpoint gene stratified by BRAF status.

Deliverables: • A table summarizing treatment burden by group (mean, median, IQR) and Mann–Whitney U statistic with p‐value.
• Bar chart & boxplot visualizing treatment burden across BRAF status.
• A results table for PDCD1, CD274, CTLA4 listing: group means, fold‐change (Mutant/Wild‐type), raw p‐value, and FDR‐adjusted p‐value.
• Boxplots of PDCD1, CD274, CTLA4 expression by BRAF status.
analysis:
Treatment Burden: BRAF-mutant and wild-type patients have nearly identical burden scores (Mutant mean=0.31, Wild-type mean=0.30), with no significant difference (Mann–Whitney U=27713.50, p=0.873).

Checkpoint Gene Expression:
• PDCD1: no significant difference (Mutant=0.172 vs Wild-type=–0.084; p=0.283, adj p=0.283).
• CD274: higher in mutants (Mutant=0.599 vs Wild-type=0.209; p=0.014, adj p=0.021; fold-change≈2.9).
• CTLA4: higher in mutants (Mutant=0.737 vs Wild-type=–0.004; p<0.001, adj p=0.001).

Overall, treatment burden does not differ by BRAF status, but CD274 and CTLA4 expression are significantly elevated in BRAF-mutant patients.

Summary of findings:

Hypothesis: BRAF-mutant melanoma patients undergo fewer treatment courses and exhibit altered immune checkpoint gene expression.

7. Perform pairwise log-rank tests or a global log-rank test across groups.  
8. Fit Cox proportional hazards model with BMI (continuous) plus covariates age_at_diagnosis and gender; extract hazard ratios and p-values.  
9. Plot KM curves and forest plot of Cox model.

Deliverables: • Table of patient counts by BMI category.  
• Kaplan–Meier survival curves by BMI group.  
• Log-rank test statistics and p-values.

analysis:

hypothesis: High expression of cell-cycle related genes predicts increased number of follow-up visits in melanoma patients.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Obtain a robust G2M_CHECKPOINT gene signature, compute per‐sample module scores, and test whether higher cell‐cycle activity (G2M score) is associated with increased follow‐up visit counts.

Steps: 1. Data loading and preprocessing:
   a. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv into a DataFrame `clin`, and cleaned_gene_expression.csv (genes×samples) into `expr`.
   b. Build a vector of patient IDs by taking the first 12 characters of each expression sample column header.
   c. In `clin`, select only the columns `bcr_patient_barcode`, `followups_count`, and `age_at_diagnosis`, and drop rows with missing `followups_count` or `age_at_diagnosis`.

2. G2M gene‐set retrieval:
   a. Call `gp.get_library_name(organism='Human')` and identify the exact MSigDB Hallmark library name (e.g. “MSigDB_Hallmark_2020”).
   b. Load that library via `gp.get_library(name=hallmark_lib, organism='Human')` into `hallmark`.
   c. List available keys with `list(hallmark.keys())` and find the key whose name contains “G2M” and “CHECKPOINT” (case‐insensitive).
   d. Extract its gene list; if the list is empty or key not found, fall back to:
      • Using the `msigdbr` package: `msigdbr(species='Homo sapiens', category='H')` and filter for `gs_name=='HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT'`.
      • Or download and parse the GMT file (h.all.v2023.symbols.gmt), find the line beginning with “HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT”, and split on tabs to get gene symbols.
   e. Verify that the retrieved G2M gene list is non‐empty and report its length.

3. Module score computation:
   a. Intersect the G2M gene list with `expr.index` (gene symbols in the expression matrix), record the number of overlapping genes.
   b. Subset `expr` to these overlapping genes and compute the per‐sample G2M module score as the mean expression across those genes.

4. Data integration:
   a. Build a DataFrame `df_scores` with columns: `sample_id`, `patient_id`, and `G2M_score`.
   b. Merge `df_scores` with the filtered `clin` on `patient_id == bcr_patient_barcode` to attach `followups_count` and `age_at_diagnosis`, then drop any rows with missing scores.
   c. Report the shape of the merged DataFrame (number of samples/patients).

5. Statistical testing and modeling:
   a. Poisson regression: fit `followups_count ~ G2M_score + age_at_diagnosis` using a GLM with a Poisson family; inspect coefficient, standard error, z‐statistic, and p‐value for `G2M_score`. Check for overdispersion; if present, refit using a Negative Binomial family.
   b. Non‐parametric comparison: median‐split `G2M_score` into high vs low groups, then perform a two‐sided Wilcoxon rank‐sum test on `followups_count` between these groups.
   c. Correlation check: compute Spearman’s rho between continuous `G2M_score` and `followups_count` with associated p‐value.

6. Visualization:
   a. Scatter plot of `followups_count` vs `G2M_score`, overlay the Poisson (or linear) fit line, and annotate with pseudo‐R² or Spearman’s rho and p‐value.
   b. Boxplot (with overlaid jittered points) comparing `followups_count` in high vs low G2M groups, annotated with the Wilcoxon p‐value.

7. Sensitivity analyses:
   a. Recompute module scores using the median instead of the mean across G2M genes and repeat steps 5b–6b.
   b. Dichotomize at upper vs lower quartiles and repeat the Wilcoxon test.

8. Reporting:
   a. Create a summary table of G2M gene set retrieval: source, library name, gene‐set key, total genes, overlapping genes.
   b. Tabulate regression results and nonparametric test statistics.
   c. Include plots and brief interpretation of whether high G2M activity predicts more follow‐up visits.

Deliverables: 1. A validated G2M gene signature listing the source, library name, gene‐set key, total genes, and number overlapping the expression data.
2. Poisson (or negative binomial) regression summary table showing the estimated effect, SE, z‐statistic, and p‐value for G2M_score.
3. Wilcoxon rank‐sum test results (U statistic and p‐value) comparing follow‐up counts in high vs low G2M groups.
4. Spearman correlation coefficient (rho) and p‐value between continuous G2M_score and followups_count.
5. Scatter plot of follow-ups vs G2M score with fit line and annotated statistics.
6. Boxplot of follow-ups by high/low G2M score with annotated Wilcoxon p‐value.
7. Sensitivity analysis results using median‐based scores and quartile splits, summarized in a short table.
8. A concise report interpreting whether elevated cell‐cycle gene expression predicts increased follow‐up frequency, including any caveats (e.g. overdispersion).
